paras: The Corning, Ohio, lynching threat was a threatened lynching in November 1888 of a Black prisoner held for the killing of Pete Donnelly, a railroad brakeman, at Corning. Lee Burrell and Mel Green, both described as "colored," were charged with the murder, and the prisoner was moved to New Lexington before a lynching party could act. The Cleveland Gazette, a Black weekly, reported that the mayor of nearby Rendville had warned Corning's officers that the town's Black residents would retaliate if the man were lynched.

Peter Donnelly, a single man who worked as a brakeman for the K. & O. Railroad, had been missing for two weeks when his body was found on Saturday, November 3, on a small island in Sunday creek near Corning. His skull was fractured in two places, and a coroner's inquest returned a verdict that he had been murdered "by some unknown person." According to a Corning dispatch in the Logan Ohio Democrat, a "colored man by the name of Burrough" was arrested at Chauncy that Saturday as someone thought "to know something of the affair," and more arrests were expected.

A wire dispatch from New Lexington dated November 9 reported that Lee Burrell and "his mistress, Mel Green, both colored," had been arrested at Chauncey on Tuesday night, November 6, charged with Donnelly's murder. The same dispatch said that Sheriff Brunner "foiled a lynching party by bringing his prisoner here" and that both prisoners denied their guilt.

The Rendville correspondent of the Cleveland Gazette gave a fuller account, writing that the prisoner had been "arrested purely on circumstantial evidence" and that residents of Corning "threatened to take him out at night and lynch him." In that account, Rendville's mayor, I. S. Tuppins, told the Corning marshal that the town's Black residents "demanded justice for one of their race" and that he would bring "a multitude of Negroes and tear the town up" if the man were lynched. The correspondent wrote that the Corning officers "consequently" carried their prisoner to New Lexington, "where he can rest in security."
No report of an indictment, trial or release of Burrell or Green appears in the coverage, and no paper names anyone in the lynching party.

White newspapers carried the story as a three-sentence wire item headed "Charged With Murder," printed on November 9 in the Maysville Evening Bulletin in Kentucky and the Clarksville Evening Chronicle in Tennessee. The brief identified the accused by race, credited the sheriff with stopping the mob and said nothing about who made up the lynching party. The Ohio Democrat's Corning report treated the case as a murder mystery and mentioned the arrest of "Burrough" but no threat of lynching.

The Cleveland Gazette ran its account on November 10 under the heading "A Brave Deed," calling the would-be lynchers "hot-headed, blood-thirsty, denizens of Corning" and giving the credit to "our fearless mayor" rather than the sheriff. It named no prisoner but reported the mayor's warning that "we were tired of being killed and no law to protect us" and that "if the law would not protect us we would protect ourselves."

The accounts differ on who was held and when: the wire named two people arrested on Tuesday night, the Ohio Democrat one man, "Burrough," arrested the previous Saturday, and the Gazette a single unnamed prisoner. No paper says whether "Burrough" and Burrell were the same man. The wire credited Sheriff Brunner with moving the prisoner, while the Gazette's correspondent credited the Corning officers acting on the mayor's warning.

bases: A lynching party threatened to take a Black prisoner held for murder out of custody and lynch him, and he was moved to New Lexington; no one was killed (A1, A4).
The papers report only a threat by a 'lynching party' of Corning residents against a prisoner accused of murder; the prisoner was moved to New Lexington and no one was killed (A1, A4).

The wire brief (A1, reprinted in A2) and the Cleveland Gazette's independent Rendville correspondent (A4) agree that a lynching was threatened against a Black prisoner held for the Corning murder and that he was taken to New Lexington, though they differ on who moved him.

accounts.label: Wire report (New Lexington)
accounts.gist: Burrell and Green, colored, were arrested at Chauncey for Donnelly's murder; Sheriff Brunner foiled a lynching party by bringing his prisoner to New Lexington; both deny guilt.

accounts.label: Corning correspondent (Ohio Democrat)
accounts.gist: Donnelly's body was found with a fractured skull, a colored man named Burrough was arrested at Chauncy, and the inquest found murder by an unknown person; no threat mentioned.

accounts.label: Black correspondent (Rendville)
accounts.gist: Corning residents threatened to lynch a Negro held on circumstantial evidence; Rendville's mayor warned the Corning marshal of Black retaliation, and the officers then took the prisoner to New Lexington.

framing.detail: Three-sentence brief headed 'Charged With Murder' naming the accused as 'colored' and crediting the sheriff; nothing on the mob.
The Logan paper's Corning dispatch treats the case as a murder mystery, 'Body of a Missing Man Found With Skull Fractured,' with no threat reported.
Headed 'A Brave Deed'; calls the would-be lynchers 'hot-headed, blood-thirsty, denizens of Corning' and praises 'our fearless mayor.'

conflicts.note: A3's dispatch is dated Nov. 5, before the Tuesday arrests in A1; it may be an earlier arrest or a variant spelling of Burrell. No paper says which.

conflicts.field: who moved the prisoner to New Lexington

versions.value: The Corning officers, after the Rendville mayor's warning to the Corning marshal

conflicts.note: A4's version comes from a Rendville correspondent praising the mayor; A1 is a one-line wire account.

record_check.dossier: Both were arrested and charged (A1), but the lynching party sought 'his prisoner' (singular, A1) and 'a Negro' (A4), most likely Burrell; Mel Green is described as his mistress. A3 names a 'Burrough' arrested earlier.
Black: both described as 'colored' (A1); the prisoner is 'a Negro' (A4).
Chauncey is the place of arrest; the threat came from residents of Corning (A4), where the murder occurred.
Date of the arrests per the wire; the threat is undated, reported Nov. 9-10. A3 reports a related arrest on Saturday, Nov. 3.
Residents of Corning ('denizens of Corning'), unnamed.
A4 credits the Corning officers acting after Rendville mayor I. S. Tuppins's warning; the record omits this Black-press account.

info: Arrests at Chauncey on Tuesday night (Nov. 6, 1888) per the wire; the threat itself is undated, before Nov. 9 dispatch
Threat by residents of Corning (A4); arrests at Chauncey/Chauncy (A1, A3); prisoner moved to New Lexington (A1, A4)
Lee Burrell and his 'mistress' Mel Green, both 'colored,' arrested; the lynching party's target is 'his prisoner' (singular) in A1 and 'a Negro' in A4
Charged with the murder of Pete (Peter) Donnelly, a railroad brakeman, at Corning; A4 calls the man 'a white man' and the evidence 'purely circumstantial'
An unnamed 'lynching party' (A1); 'hot-headed, blood-thirsty, denizens of Corning' (A4)
Prisoner held at New Lexington; both accused denied guilt; no later outcome found
